description_full: Vericel Corporation, a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company, engages in the research, development, manufacture, and distribution of cellular therapies and specialty biologic products for sports medicine and severe burn care markets in North America. The company markets autologous cell therapy products comprising MACI, an autologous cultured chondrocytes on porcine collagen membrane for the repair of symptomatic, and single or multiple full-thickness cartilage defects of the knee; Epicel, a permanent skin replacement humanitarian use device for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients with deep-dermal or full-thickness burns; and NexoBrid, a biological orphan product for eschar removal in adults and pediatric patients with deep partial-thickness and/or full-thickness thermal burns. Vericel Corporation was formerly known as Aastrom Biosciences, Inc. and changed its name to Vericel Corporation in November 2014. The company was incorporated in 1989 and is headquartered in Burlington, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Mr. Dominick C. Colangelo Esq. | CEO, President & Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $1.7M (FY2025)

CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: Vericel Corporation is a mid-cap healthcare business with a $2.9B market cap on $276M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years and +18% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +11524.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at -7% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 67% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $25M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 18× is fortress-like.

Net dilution runs at 0.5% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and stock-based comp at 14% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
